content: 1. Some healthcare providers viewed mobile phones as a form of supervision, while others believed they enhanced performance and care delivery. This perception motivated some providers, but others felt guilty when they failed to deliver adequate care. (Jones, 2012) 2. The use of mobile health technologies enabled some healthcare providers to feel connected to their peers within their organizations, which was perceived as supportive. However, in one study, providers still expressed the need for face-to-face interactions with their colleagues. (Barnabee, 2014; Hampshire, 2016; Henry, 2016; Jennings, 2013; Madon, 2014; Valaitis, 2005) 3. Mobile health technologies facilitated two-way communication between healthcare providers and clients, keeping providers informed about clients’ conditions. This was seen as improving immediacy of care, follow-up for missing clients, informed care, and emotional support, even in the absence of physical contact. However, some cases still required face-to-face interactions. (Barnabee, 2014; Chang, 2011; Hampshire, 2016; Hirsch-Moverman, 2017; Huq, 2014; Jennings, 2013) 4. Healthcare providers had mixed reactions to being contactable via mobile health technologies outside of working hours. While some found it useful for emergencies, others were ambivalent or negative about being contacted after hours. Some suggested setting boundaries to protect their personal time. (Chang, 2011; Hampshire, 2016; Huq, 2014; Jennings, 2013; Valaitis, 2005) 5. Mobile health technologies allowed healthcare providers to expand their range of tasks, including taking on responsibilities previously assigned to higher-level workers and performing tasks independently. This was experienced as fulfilling by both those who gained and those who delegated tasks. Some providers noted that clients with mobile phones often contacted lay health workers first, allowing professionals to focus on underserved areas. (Barnabee, 2014; Chang, 2011; Khan, 2015; Praveen, 2014) 6. Some healthcare providers found it challenging to explain or act on information received via mobile devices when it exceeded their clinical capacity or when follow-up support was unavailable. (Orchard, 2014; Praveen, 2014) 7. Many healthcare providers perceived mobile health technologies as increasing efficiency due to the speed at which they could work. However, some participants did not find it efficient, as it did not reduce their workload, and others felt it increased their workload. (Ayiasi, 2015; Barnabee, 2014; Chang, 2011; Hampshire, 2016; Hao, 2015; Huq, 2014; Jennings, 2013; Jones, 2012; Madon, 2014) 8. The use of mobile health technologies for record-keeping was seen as helpful for decision-making and information sharing by healthcare providers and managers. (Khan, 2015; Madon, 2014; Murray, 2011) 9. Healthcare providers working in rural or geographically challenging areas appreciated the efficiency of mobile health technologies in delivering services despite these challenges. In urban settings, these technologies saved travel time, allowing more time with clients. (Chang, 2011; Hampshire, 2016; Hirsch-Moverman, 2017; Valaitis, 2005) 10. Providers valued the portability of mobile health technologies, which allowed them to work flexibly and access information without being office-bound. (Hampshire, 2016; Murray, 2011; Orchard, 2014; Valaitis, 2005) 11. Some providers expressed dissatisfaction with mobile health technologies when changes were introduced too rapidly or when the technologies did not meet their expectations. (Hao, 2015; Valaitis, 2005) 12. Mobile health interventions often required client registration, which some providers viewed as a menial task inappropriate for their job level, leading to dissatisfaction and perceptions of increased workload. (Hirsch-Moverman, 2017; Medhanyie, 2015; Wolf-Piggott, 2017) 13. Some mobile health interventions included treatment algorithms on devices, which providers found useful for guiding care delivery. However, others felt the algorithms were too prescriptive and feared losing clinical competencies by relying on them. (Mitchell, 2012; Orchard, 2014; Shao, 2014; Surka, 2014) 14. Some providers experienced anxiety when learning to use mobile health technologies. Training and familiarity helped alleviate this anxiety, but providers felt hindered if their clinical mentors did not use the technologies. (Hirsch-Moverman, 2017; Madon, 2014; Mitchell, 2012; Murray, 2011; Praveen, 2014) 15. Both lay and professional healthcare providers required technical support when navigating mobile health technologies. Support was sometimes provided by higher-level staff or through peer-to-peer assistance. (Hao, 2015; Madon, 2014; Murray, 2011) 16. Providers’ level of techno-literacy influenced their perceptions of mobile health technologies. Those proficient in using the technologies had positive views, while those who struggled were more likely to perceive them negatively and worry about errors. Poor techno-literacy sometimes threatened job security. (Hao, 2015; Hirsch-Moverman, 2017; Madon, 2014) 17. Providers were conscious of protecting client confidentiality when using mobile health technologies, especially for stigmatized conditions like HIV/AIDS. Measures to ensure confidentiality were often negotiated between providers and clients. (Hirsch-Moverman, 2017; Valaitis, 2005; Wolf-Piggott, 2017) 18. In some primary healthcare programs, providers used their personal mobile phones and internet access for work purposes. This raised concerns about the costs of airtime and charging devices, though some providers felt a moral obligation to assist clients using their own resources. (Hampshire, 2016; Jennings, 2013; Quinn, 2013) 19. Providers consistently highlighted the advantages of mobile health technologies over paper-based systems, including quicker record-keeping, easier access to client data, and simpler error correction. However, some providers disliked maintaining both digital and paper systems. (Madon, 2014; Mitchell, 2012; Shao, 2014) 20. Providers believed mobile health interventions positively influenced clients’ health behaviors, improving responsiveness and treatment adherence. Some also felt that visual displays on devices helped clients better understand their conditions. (Barnabee, 2014; Chang, 2011; Huq, 2014) 21. Some providers reported that mobile health technologies enhanced their social status and increased trust and respect from clients and communities. Lay health workers, in particular, felt the devices improved their standing among health professionals. (Ayiasi, 2015; Barnabee, 2014; Jones, 2012) 22. Some providers were concerned that the use of expensive devices could exacerbate inequities between themselves and their colleagues or clients, potentially creating a social gap. (Valaitis, 2005) 23. Clients perceived providers’ use of digital devices as leading to better care, believing it made providers more thorough in their assessments. (Jones, 2012; Khan, 2015) 24. Providers had mixed views on the increased workload from mobile health interventions. Some felt the additional work was not appreciated by supervisors, while others expected compensation for the extra effort. (Hao, 2015; Praveen, 2014) 25. Contextual issues, such as language barriers, client poverty, gender discrimination, and staff shortages, affected providers’ experiences with mobile health technologies. These issues sometimes hindered the optimization of the technologies’ benefits. (Chang, 2011; Huq, 2014) 26. Providers suggested improvements to mobile health interventions, including involving them in planning and decision-making, providing airtime, simplifying software, and improving connectivity. They also recommended durable devices, color displays, and solar chargers. (Madon, 2014)
